description: Build and data generation scripts: OCV generation, ASHRAE reference data, OCHRE BESTEST runner, ResStock download, SI guard, ticket verification, and stream filter.

reviews.title: gen_ocv.py: PyBaMM chemistry parameter sets and stoichiometry verification
reviews.prompt: gen_ocv.py generates open-circuit voltage (OCV) curves for lithium-ion battery chemistries using PyBaMM parameter sets. Verify: (a) Chen2020 parameter set for NMC811: cathode stoichiometry range (typically 0.4-0.95 for NMC811), anode stoichiometry (graphite, typically 0.01-0.9), and OCV curve shape (characteristic voltage plateau at ~3.65V for NMC). Verify the PyBaMM parameter ID or file path is correct—a mis-versioned parameter set from PyBaMM could use older Chen 2017 parameters instead of 2020. (b) Prada2013 parameter set for LFP: LFP has an extremely flat OCV curve (3.2-3.45V across most of SOC range) which creates unique SOC estimation challenges. Verify the OCV curve captures this flatness correctly and that the voltage resolution is sufficient—2 mV errors in OCV can produce 10% SOC errors for LFP. (c) NCA_Kim2011 parameter set for NCA: cathode stoichiometry range, OCV curve shape with characteristic slope (no flat plateau unlike LFP). Verify the Kim2011 parameters match the original publication. (d) LTO OCP from Colclasure 2011: LTO (lithium titanate) anode has a very flat OCP at ~1.55V vs Li/Li+. Verify the Colclasure 2011 parameters are correctly sourced and the OCP curve shape is correct—LTO has extremely high rate capability due to zero-strain intercalation. (e) Stoichiometry matching: for each chemistry, the cathode and anode stoichiometry windows must be matched so that the full-cell voltage range (4.2V max to 2.5V min typical) corresponds to the correct SOC range. Mismatched stoichiometry shifts the entire OCV-SOC curve, causing systematic SOC estimation errors of 5-15%. (f) Verify the output format (CSV or TOML) matches what the Rust battery model expects for OCV curve loading.

reviews.title: gen_ashrae_reference.py: every formula verified against ASHRAE HOF 2021
reviews.prompt: gen_ashrae_reference.py is 1023 lines and generates the reference JSON used for ALL parity tests. This is the single most critical script in the repository—an error here propagates to every test. Verify every formula against ASHRAE HOF 2021: (a) Film resistances: interior surface film (R_si) and exterior surface film (R_se). ASHRAE HOF Ch.26 Table 1: R_si = 0.12 m²·K/W for vertical surfaces (walls), 0.10 for upward heat flow (ceilings), 0.16 for downward (floors). Exterior varies: R_se = 0.03 for wind > 6.7 m/s, 0.04 for wind < 6.7 m/s. Verify these are correct for each boundary orientation. (b) Layer R-values: for each material layer, R = thickness / conductivity. Verify conductivity values from HOF Ch.26 Table 4. Common values: gypsum board k=0.16 W/(m·K), fiberglass batt k=0.036-0.045, plywood k=0.12, concrete k=1.4-2.0, XPS k=0.029. (c) Window U-factor: per NFRC rating or ASHRAE HOF Ch.15 methodology. Center-glass U-factor + edge effects + frame effects. Verify the glazing layer count, low-e coatings, and gas fill (argon, krypton) are correctly parameterized. (d) Assembly capacitance: per ASHRAE HOF Ch.18, the effective capacitance for a multi-layer wall depends on the layer ordering. Layers on the interior side of the insulation contribute more to interior-side thermal mass than layers on the exterior side. Verify the capacitance computation accounts for this distribution. (e) Node count: the RC network discretization in the reference must match the HARES RC network node count and layout exactly—if the reference uses more nodes, the parity test will fail due to discretization error, not physics error. (f) All inline citations to ASHRAE HOF 2021 must be correct (correct chapter, table, equation number). A miscited formula could be based on the wrong ASHRAE edition with different values. (g) Verify the output JSON schema matches what the parity test harness expects—any schema mismatch will cause all parity tests to fail.

reviews.title: ochre_bestest_600.py: OCHRE-side BESTEST runner geometry and materials
reviews.prompt: ochre_bestest_600.py runs BESTEST-600 cases on the OCHRE model to serve as one side of the HARES-OCHRE parity comparison. Verify that the OCHRE-side runner uses exactly the same inputs as the HARES-side BESTEST test: (a) Building geometry: BESTEST Case 600 is a simple rectangular building 8m wide × 6m deep × 2.7m high, with two south-facing windows of 3 m² each. Interior volume, floor area, window area, and exterior surface areas must match exactly between OCHRE and HARES runs. A 1% difference in window area changes solar gain by 1%, which compounds over the annual simulation. (b) Materials: BESTEST defines lightweight and heavyweight construction cases with specific layer composition. Case 600 uses lightweight walls: 13 mm plasterboard + 66 mm fiberglass + 13 mm wood siding. Verify materials and thicknesses are identical. (c) Boundary conditions: interior convection coefficients, exterior convection (constant vs wind-driven), radiative exchange with sky and ground. Verify these are set identically. (d) Weather data: BESTEST uses a simple annual weather file (typically TMY or synthetic with sinusoidal outdoor temperature, no solar for Case 600 to isolate conduction). Verify the weather file is identical. (e) Internal gains: BESTEST defines constant internal gains (200 W convective) with no occupant variability for the base case. Verify these are set identically. (f) Simulation settings: timestep (typically 1 hour for BESTEST), warmup period, solver tolerances. Verify these match. Any discrepancy between the OCHRE and HARES BESTEST setups invalidates the parity comparison—a difference attributed to the physics model might actually be an input difference.

reviews.title: download_resstock_fixtures.py: S3 download robustness and fixture coverage
reviews.prompt: download_resstock_fixtures.py downloads ResStock building fixture files from S3 (or equivalent storage). Verify download robustness: (a) Retries: S3 downloads can fail transiently (network errors, throttling, temporary S3 unavailability). Verify the script implements retries with exponential backoff (e.g., 3 retries at 1s, 2s, 4s delays). (b) Checksums: after download, each file's integrity should be verified with a checksum (MD5, SHA256, or ETag). Without checksum verification, a truncated or corrupted download will produce silently wrong building fixtures that generate incorrect simulation results. Verify the checksums are stored in a manifest file and regenerated when the upstream data changes. (c) Fixture selection: the downloaded fixtures must cover all climate zones (IECC 1A through 8), building types (single-family detached, attached, apartment, manufactured), equipment combinations (all fuel types for heating, all WH types, with/without PV, with/without EV), and vintages (pre-1980 through 2020+). A gap in fixture coverage means certain dwelling configurations are never tested. (d) Verify that the script does not download the entire ResStock dataset (which can be 500+ GB) but selects a representative sample. The selection criteria should be documented and reproducible. (e) Error handling: if a download fails after retries, does the script continue with remaining fixtures or exit? A partial fixture set is better than no fixtures, as long as the missing files are clearly reported. (f) Verify the script works on both Linux and macOS CI runners—S3 client library (boto3) version compatibility, filesystem path handling, and available disk space checks.

reviews.title: check-si-guard.sh: grep patterns and false positive handling for IP units
reviews.prompt: check-si-guard.sh is a CI guard script that prevents Imperial (IP) units from entering the codebase. Verify its grep patterns: (a) Pattern coverage: BTU, F (Fahrenheit), lb (pound-mass), ft (feet), inch/in, mph, psf, psi, gallon/gal, cfm, and any other IP units. Verify all common IP unit strings are covered. Missing patterns allow IP units to slip through. (b) False positive handling: the string 'F' appears in many non-unit contexts (e.g., 'F' as a variable name for force, 'F' in error messages 'FAILED', 'F' as hexadecimal digit). Similarly 'ft' appears in words like 'left', 'after', 'offset'. Verify the grep patterns are specific enough to avoid flagging every occurrence of these common letter sequences—regex word boundaries ( ) or surrounding whitespace/punctuation qualifiers should be used. (c) Comments and string literals: IP units in comments (e.g., '// convert from BTU to J') or string literals (e.g., '\"Temperature: 72 F\"') should arguably be allowed since they don't affect simulation math. Verify the script either excludes comments/strings or documents them as intentionally flagged. (d) Allowed exceptions: some files (e.g., scripts that parse legacy files, unit conversion tables) legitimately contain IP units. Verify there is an allowlist mechanism (by file path glob or inline annotation like '// SI-GUARD-IGNORE: EnergyPlus reference value'). (e) Verify the grep itself uses correct flags: -E for extended regex, -r for recursive, -n for line numbers. Check that the error message is clear and actionable—the developer should see the exact line with the offending unit. (f) CI integration: verify the script exits non-zero when violations are found and produces a parsable output format (e.g., GitHub Actions annotations via ::error file=FILENAME::MESSAGE).

reviews.title: verify-tickets.sh and verify-ticket-prompt.md: ticket verification completeness
reviews.prompt: verify-tickets.sh orchestrates ticket verification across all review categories. Verify: (a) Coverage of all review categories: the script must discover all JSON manifest files in scripts/reviews/ and verify tickets for each review ID. Verify the discovery mechanism (glob for *.json) correctly finds all manifests and parses the 'reviews' array. (b) Ticket output discovery: the script must find all generated ticket markdown files in the tickets/ directory (or wherever tickets are written). Verify that the glob/naming convention for ticket files matches what the verification agent produces—a mismatch between expected and actual ticket filenames would cause all tickets to appear missing. (c) verify-ticket-prompt.md: this prompt template defines how the AI agent verifies each ticket. Verify it includes checks for: ticket completeness (all sections filled), ticket accuracy (findings match the source code), severity classification, and references (file paths, line numbers). (d) Failure reporting: if a ticket is missing or incomplete, the script should exit non-zero and produce a clear report of which tickets failed. (e) Idempotency: running verify-tickets.sh twice should produce the same result (no side effects from the first run). (f) Verify that the script does not require any credentials or API keys to run—if it needs an LLM API key, this should be documented and the script should gracefully skip with a clear message when the key is absent.

reviews.title: stream-filter.sh: edge cases for CI pipeline input processing
reviews.prompt: stream-filter.sh is a CI pipeline utility that filters/transforms data streams (stdin to stdout). Review edge case handling: (a) Empty input: if stdin is empty (0 bytes), the script should produce empty output (or the identity output for the transformation) without error. An empty input should not cause a division-by-zero or sed/awk syntax error. (b) Long lines: CI build logs can contain very long lines (compiler error paths, JSON blobs). Verify the script handles lines longer than the system's ARG_MAX or the tool's internal buffer—sed, awk, and grep have varying line-length limits. (c) Binary data: if binary garbage appears in the input (e.g., a corrupted log file), the script should not crash or produce garbled output—it should either pass through or filter out non-UTF-8 sequences gracefully. (d) Input interleaving: if the script processes multiple input streams or handles concurrent writes (e.g., stdout and stderr merged), verify the output ordering is preserved. (e) Performance: verify the script uses efficient streaming (line-by-line, not reading the entire input into memory). A script that buffers all input before output causes OOM on large build logs. (f) Pipeline composition: verify the script can be composed with other commands via pipes without issues—some scripts using `read` in a subshell can break pipeline composition. (g) Verify the shebang is correct (#!/bin/bash vs #!/bin/sh) and that the script uses only POSIX-compatible features if it claims /bin/sh compatibility. (h) Check the exit code: the script should exit 0 on success and non-zero on processing error, following standard Unix conventions.
